levels.title: LEVEL 0: Absolute Computer and Programming Basics
levels.description: This level focuses on understanding computers, programs, Java, and beginner vocabulary. Lessons use simple explanations, analogies, Java examples, mistakes, quizzes, and practical tasks.
outcomes: Explain the concept in simple words
Read and dry-run a Java example
Avoid common beginner and professional mistakes
Apply the idea in a small exercise
Connect the idea to scalable code

lessons.title: What is a computer program?
lessons.simpleExplanation: What is a computer program? belongs to Absolute Computer and Programming Basics. In simple words, it is a tool or idea that helps you understanding computers, programs, Java, and beginner vocabulary. Learn the plain meaning first, then connect it to a tiny Java example, then use it in a small task.
lessons.explainLikeTen: Imagine you are teaching a younger friend. The idea called What is a computer program? has one job. You do not need to learn everything at once. First ask: what problem does this solve, what does it look like in Java, and what tiny mistake should I avoid?
lessons.realLifeAnalogy: Think of What is a computer program? as one tool in a developer toolbox. A professional chooses the right tool, gives it a clear name, and keeps it separate from unrelated work.

deepDiveSections.title: Why This Matters
deepDiveSections.body: What is a computer program? matters because it helps you build skill in understanding computers, programs, Java, and beginner vocabulary. A job-ready developer does not only ask whether code runs. They ask whether the next developer can understand it, test it, and change it without breaking other parts.

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model
deepDiveSections.body: Use this mental model: name the input, name the work, name the output. For What is a computer program?, pause before coding and say what value enters the code, what decision or transformation happens, and what result should come out.

deepDiveSections.title: Scalable Code Angle
deepDiveSections.body: When What is a computer program? appears in a larger project, keep it close to the class or method that owns the rule. Avoid spreading the same rule across many screens, menus, or files. One clear home for one rule makes changes safer.

deepDiveSections.title: Interview Explanation
deepDiveSections.body: If an interviewer asks about What is a computer program?, explain it in this order: simple definition, tiny Java example, common mistake, and one real project use. This proves understanding instead of memorization.

lessons.jobUse: What is a computer program? appears in onboarding tasks, console tools, scripts, form handling, and every beginner project where data must be named, printed, or read.
masteryChecklist: I can explain What is a computer program? without using memorized textbook language.
I can write a tiny example from memory.
I can dry-run the example line by line.
I can name one common mistake and how to fix it.
I can say how this idea belongs in a clean, changeable project.
dryRun: Step 1: Read the goal: what should What is a computer program? produce or protect?
Step 2: List the values before the code starts.
Step 3: Move one line at a time and update the values by hand.
Step 4: Compare your predicted output with the actual output.
Step 5: If they differ, find the first line where your prediction changed.
lineByLine: Read the code from top to bottom because Java executes statements in order.
Notice the names. Good names explain the purpose before you even read the details.
Watch the braces. Braces show which lines belong together.
Connect each line back to What is a computer program?: ask what value is created, changed, checked, or printed.
For scalable code, separate input, processing, and output when the example grows.
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize What is a computer program? without explaining the simple purpose first.
Changing many lines at once, then not knowing which change caused the problem.
Using unclear names like a, b, x, and temp when the value has a real meaning.
Ignoring compiler errors instead of reading them as clues.
Mixing unrelated responsibilities in one large block of code.
lessons.miniPractice: In your own words, explain What is a computer program?. Then write or read a tiny Java example and predict the output before looking at the answer.

quiz.question: What is the simplest useful way to think about What is a computer program??
options: A Java idea that solves a specific kind of problem
A random word that must be memorized only
A paid online service
Something that cannot be practiced
quiz.explanation: What is a computer program? is useful because it helps solve a real programming problem.

quiz.question: Which habit makes What is a computer program? easier to learn?
options: Copy code without reading it
Read the example line by line and predict the output
Ignore mistakes
Use bigger code before understanding smaller code
quiz.explanation: Line-by-line reading builds the same mental model Java uses when it runs code.

quiz.question: What is a professional habit when using What is a computer program??
options: Put every idea in one giant method
Use confusing names
Keep responsibilities separate and names clear
Avoid testing
quiz.explanation: Scalable code is easier to change when each block has one clear responsibility.

quiz.question: What should you do when code about What is a computer program? gives an error?
options: Delete everything immediately
Read the error, check the line, and test one small fix
Add random symbols
Never run the code again
quiz.explanation: Debugging is controlled investigation. Small fixes teach you more than random changes.

quiz.question: Which next step turns What is a computer program? from theory into skill?
options: Build a tiny working example
Only watch videos
Skip practice
Wait until advanced topics
quiz.explanation: A tiny working example gives your brain a concrete memory of the concept.

quiz.question: A teammate says their What is a computer program? code works but is hard to change. What should you check first?
options: Whether the code has clear names and one responsibility per method
Whether the file is as long as possible
Whether all logic is hidden in main
Whether there are no examples or tests
quiz.explanation: Maintainability starts with names, focused responsibilities, and behavior that can be checked.

quiz.question: Which debugging move is best for a broken What is a computer program? example?
options: Rewrite the entire program without reading the error
Add random code until the error disappears
Create a smaller failing example and inspect values step by step
Assume Java is wrong
quiz.explanation: A smaller failing example removes noise and helps you find the real mistake.

quiz.question: When should you reveal the solution for a What is a computer program? exercise?
options: Before reading the problem
After making a real attempt, writing a prediction, and checking hints
Only after copying someone else's answer
Never, because feedback is useless
quiz.explanation: Learning sticks when you struggle productively first, then compare your approach with a clean solution.

codingChallenge.prompt: Create a small Java example for What is a computer program?. First solve it directly, then ask how you would split the code if this became part of a larger app.
codingChallenge.expectedOutput: A clear result that proves your What is a computer program? code ran correctly.
hints: Write the expected output before writing the code.
Use clear variable and method names.
After it works, ask which lines belong together and which lines should be separated.

solutions.title: Direct beginner solution
solutions.explanation: Use this when the problem is tiny and you are learning the idea for the first time.

solutions.title: Method-based solution
solutions.explanation: Move the useful work into a method so it has a name and can be reused or tested.

solutions.title: Scalable service-style solution
solutions.explanation: For real apps, keep business logic away from input/output so one change does not break the whole program.

deepDiveSections.title: Why This Matters
deepDiveSections.body: Comparison operators matters because it helps you build skill in using symbols that calculate, compare, assign, and combine logic. A job-ready developer does not only ask whether code runs. They ask whether the next developer can understand it, test it, and change it without breaking other parts.

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model

A job-ready developer does not only ask whether code runs. They ask whether the next developer can understand it, test it, and change it without breaking other parts.

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model
deepDiveSections.body: Use this mental model: name the input, name the work, name the output. For Single responsibility in methods, pause before coding and say what value enters the code, what decision or transformation happens, and what result should come out.

deepDiveSections.title: Scalable Code Angle
deepDiveSections.body: When Single responsibility in methods appears in a larger project, keep it close to the class or method that owns the rule. Avoid spreading the same rule across many screens, menus, or files. One clear home for one rule makes changes safer.

deepDiveSections.title: Interview Explanation

lessons.explainLikeTen: Imagine you are teaching a younger friend. The idea called Method overriding has one job. You do not need to learn everything at once. First ask: what problem does this solve, what does it look like in Java, and what tiny mistake should I avoid?

deepDiveSections.title: Why This Matters
deepDiveSections.body: Method overriding matters because it helps you build skill in protecting code and using abstraction to keep systems flexible. A job-ready developer does not only ask whether code runs. They ask whether the next developer can understand it, test it, and change it without breaking other parts.

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model
deepDiveSections.body: Use this mental model: name the input, name the work, name the output. For Method overriding, pause before coding and say what value enters the code, what decision or transformation happens, and what result should come out.

deepDiveSections.title: Scalable Code Angle
deepDiveSections.body: When Method overriding appears in a larger project, keep it close to the class or method that owns the rule. Avoid spreading the same rule across many screens, menus, or files. One clear home for one rule makes changes safer.

deepDiveSections.title: Interview Explanation

deepDiveSections.title: Why This Matters

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model
deepDiveSections.body: Use this mental model: name the input, name the work, name the output. For try, pause before coding and say what value enters the code, what decision or transformation happens, and what result should come out.

deepDiveSections.title: Scalable Code Angle
deepDiveSections.body: When try appears in a larger project, keep it close to the class or method that owns the rule. Avoid spreading the same rule across many screens, menus, or files. One clear home for one rule makes changes safer.

deepDiveSections.title: Interview Explanation

lessons.jobUse: try appears in real application models, service layers, payment rules, permissions, exception-safe workflows, and collection-heavy features.

lineByLine: Read the code from top to bottom because Java executes statements in order.

For scalable code, separate input, processing, and output when the example grows.

masteryChecklist: I can explain JUnit without using memorized textbook language.
I can write a tiny example from memory.
I can dry-run the example line by line.
I can name one common mistake and how to fix it.
I can say how this idea belongs in a clean, changeable project.
dryRun: Step 1: Read the goal: what should JUnit produce or protect?
Step 2: List the values before the code starts.
Step 3: Move one line at a time and update the values by hand.
Step 4: Compare your predicted output with the actual output.
Step 5: If they differ, find the first line where your prediction changed.
lineByLine: Read the code from top to bottom because Java executes statements in order.
Notice the names. Good names explain the purpose before you even read the details.
Watch the braces. Braces show which lines belong together.
Connect each line back to JUnit: ask what value is created, changed, checked, or printed.
For scalable code, separate input, processing, and output when the example grows.
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize JUnit without explaining the simple purpose first.
Changing many lines at once, then not knowing which change caused the problem.
Using unclear names like a, b, x, and temp when the value has a real meaning.
Ignoring compiler errors instead of reading them as clues.
Mixing unrelated responsibilities in one large block of code.
lessons.miniPractice: In your own words, explain JUnit. Then write or read a tiny Java example and predict the output before looking at the answer.

quiz.question: What is the simplest useful way to think about JUnit?
options: A Java idea that solves a specific kind of problem
A random word that must be memorized only
A paid online service
Something that cannot be practiced
quiz.explanation: JUnit is useful because it helps solve a real programming problem.

quiz.question: Which habit makes JUnit easier to learn?
options: Copy code without reading it
Read the example line by line and predict the output
Ignore mistakes
Use bigger code before understanding smaller code
quiz.explanation: Line-by-line reading builds the same mental model Java uses when it runs code.

quiz.question: What is a professional habit when using JUnit?
options: Put every idea in one giant method
Use confusing names
Keep responsibilities separate and names clear
Avoid testing
quiz.explanation: Scalable code is easier to change when each block has one clear responsibility.

quiz.question: What should you do when code about JUnit gives an error?
options: Delete everything immediately
Read the error, check the line, and test one small fix
Add random symbols
Never run the code again
quiz.explanation: Debugging is controlled investigation. Small fixes teach you more than random changes.

quiz.question: Which next step turns JUnit from theory into skill?
options: Build a tiny working example
Only watch videos
Skip practice
Wait until advanced topics
quiz.explanation: A tiny working example gives your brain a concrete memory of the concept.

quiz.question: A teammate says their JUnit code works but is hard to change. What should you check first?
options: Whether the code has clear names and one responsibility per method
Whether the file is as long as possible
Whether all logic is hidden in main
Whether there are no examples or tests
quiz.explanation: Maintainability starts with names, focused responsibilities, and behavior that can be checked.

quiz.question: Which debugging move is best for a broken JUnit example?
options: Rewrite the entire program without reading the error
Add random code until the error disappears
Create a smaller failing example and inspect values step by step
Assume Java is wrong
quiz.explanation: A smaller failing example removes noise and helps you find the real mistake.

quiz.question: When should you reveal the solution for a JUnit exercise?
options: Before reading the problem
After making a real attempt, writing a prediction, and checking hints
Only after copying someone else's answer
Never, because feedback is useless
quiz.explanation: Learning sticks when you struggle productively first, then compare your approach with a clean solution.

codingChallenge.prompt: Create a small Java example for JUnit. First solve it directly, then ask how you would split the code if this became part of a larger app.
codingChallenge.expectedOutput: A clear result that proves your JUnit code ran correctly.
hints: Write the expected output before writing the code.
Use clear variable and method names.
After it works, ask which lines belong together and which lines should be separated.

solutions.title: Direct beginner solution
solutions.explanation: Use this when the problem is tiny and you are learning the idea for the first time.

solutions.title: Method-based solution
solutions.explanation: Move the useful work into a method so it has a name and can be reused or tested.

solutions.title: Scalable service-style solution
solutions.explanation: For real apps, keep business logic away from input/output so one change does not break the whole program.

lessons.explainLikeTen: Imagine you are teaching a younger friend. The idea called Activity has one job. You do not need to learn everything at once. First ask: what problem does this solve, what does it look like in Java, and what tiny mistake should I avoid?
lessons.realLifeAnalogy: An Android app is like a small shop. The screen is the front counter, the ViewModel is the manager, and the repository talks to storage or the network.

deepDiveSections.title: Why This Matters
deepDiveSections.body: Activity matters because it helps you build skill in connecting Java knowledge to Android app development. A job-ready developer does not only ask whether code runs. They ask whether the next developer can understand it, test it, and change it without breaking other parts.

deepDiveSections.title: Mental Model
deepDiveSections.body: Use this mental model: name the input, name the work, name the output. For Activity, pause before coding and say what value enters the code, what decision or transformation happens, and what result should come out.

deepDiveSections.title: Scalable Code Angle
deepDiveSections.body: When Activity appears in a larger project, keep it close to the class or method that owns the rule. Avoid spreading the same rule across many screens, menus, or files. One clear home for one rule makes changes safer.

deepDiveSections.title: Interview Explanation
deepDiveSections.body: If an interviewer asks about Activity, explain it in this order: simple definition, tiny Java example, common mistake, and one real project use. This proves understanding instead of memorization.

lessons.jobUse: Activity appears in Android apps, interview tasks, data-structure problem solving, portfolio projects, modern Java, and enterprise Java direction.
masteryChecklist: I can explain Activity without using memorized textbook language.
I can write a tiny example from memory.
I can dry-run the example line by line.
I can name one common mistake and how to fix it.
I can say how this idea belongs in a clean, changeable project.
dryRun: Step 1: Read the goal: what should Activity produce or protect?
Step 2: List the values before the code starts.
Step 3: Move one line at a time and update the values by hand.
Step 4: Compare your predicted output with the actual output.
Step 5: If they differ, find the first line where your prediction changed.
lineByLine: Read the code from top to bottom because Java executes statements in order.
Notice the names. Good names explain the purpose before you even read the details.
Watch the braces. Braces show which lines belong together.
Connect each line back to Activity: ask what value is created, changed, checked, or printed.
For scalable code, separate input, processing, and output when the example grows.
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize Activity without explaining the simple purpose first.
Changing many lines at once, then not knowing which change caused the problem.
Using unclear names like a, b, x, and temp when the value has a real meaning.
Ignoring compiler errors instead of reading them as clues.
Mixing unrelated responsibilities in one large block of code.
lessons.miniPractice: In your own words, explain Activity. Then write or read a tiny Java example and predict the output before looking at the answer.

quiz.question: What is the simplest useful way to think about Activity?
options: A Java idea that solves a specific kind of problem
A random word that must be memorized only
A paid online service
Something that cannot be practiced
quiz.explanation: Activity is useful because it helps solve a real programming problem.

quiz.question: Which habit makes Activity easier to learn?
options: Copy code without reading it
Read the example line by line and predict the output
Ignore mistakes
Use bigger code before understanding smaller code
quiz.explanation: Line-by-line reading builds the same mental model Java uses when it runs code.

quiz.question: What is a professional habit when using Activity?
options: Put every idea in one giant method
Use confusing names
Keep responsibilities separate and names clear
Avoid testing
quiz.explanation: Scalable code is easier to change when each block has one clear responsibility.

quiz.question: What should you do when code about Activity gives an error?
options: Delete everything immediately
Read the error, check the line, and test one small fix
Add random symbols
Never run the code again
quiz.explanation: Debugging is controlled investigation. Small fixes teach you more than random changes.

quiz.question: Which next step turns Activity from theory into skill?
options: Build a tiny working example
Only watch videos
Skip practice
Wait until advanced topics
quiz.explanation: A tiny working example gives your brain a concrete memory of the concept.

quiz.question: A teammate says their Activity code works but is hard to change. What should you check first?
options: Whether the code has clear names and one responsibility per method
Whether the file is as long as possible
Whether all logic is hidden in main
Whether there are no examples or tests
quiz.explanation: Maintainability starts with names, focused responsibilities, and behavior that can be checked.

quiz.question: Which debugging move is best for a broken Activity example?
options: Rewrite the entire program without reading the error
Add random code until the error disappears
Create a smaller failing example and inspect values step by step
Assume Java is wrong
quiz.explanation: A smaller failing example removes noise and helps you find the real mistake.

quiz.question: When should you reveal the solution for a Activity exercise?
options: Before reading the problem
After making a real attempt, writing a prediction, and checking hints
Only after copying someone else's answer
Never, because feedback is useless
quiz.explanation: Learning sticks when you struggle productively first, then compare your approach with a clean solution.

codingChallenge.expectedOutput: A clear result that proves your Activity code ran correctly.
hints: Write the expected output before writing the code.
Use clear variable and method names.
After it works, ask which lines belong together and which lines should be separated.

solutions.title: Method-based solution

solutions.title: Scalable service-style solution
solutions.explanation: For real apps, keep business logic away from input/output so one change does not break the whole program.

constraints: Use clear names that describe the meaning of the value.
Keep one method focused on one job.
Print or return a result that can be checked.
Do not use advanced shortcuts before the simple version is clear.
The solution must demonstrate Real-life decision examples, not only print a hardcoded sentence.
hints: Write one expected output line first.
Start with the simplest version that works.
Refactor into a method or service when the code grows.
Use names that describe the real meaning of the data.
practiceExercises.expectedOutput: A visible result proving Real-life decision examples works.
dryRun: Write the starting values.
Run the first line mentally.
Update one value at a time.
Stop at each condition or loop and choose the next path.
Explain how the final output proves Real-life decision examples worked.

commonWrongSolutions.title: Hardcoded-only answer
commonWrongSolutions.explanation: This is wrong because it avoids practicing Real-life decision examples. It prints a phrase but does not show the rule, data, decision, or structure.

commonWrongSolutions.title: Giant mixed method
commonWrongSolutions.explanation: This may run, but it mixes setup, rule, output, and future changes in one place. That becomes painful when the project grows.

tradeOffs: A direct solution is faster to write and easier for beginners to inspect.
A method-based solution is easier to test and reuse.
A service-style solution is better when this logic becomes part of a larger app.
Avoid adding abstractions before you understand the simple version.
rubric: Correctness: the output proves Real-life decision examples is being used correctly.
Readability: names explain purpose without extra comments.
Structure: each method or class has one main responsibility.
Testing idea: you can name at least one input that should pass and one that should fail.
Change safety: one small rule change should not require editing unrelated code.

solutions.title: Direct beginner solution
solutions.explanation: Use this when the problem is tiny and you are learning the idea for the first time.

solutions.title: Method-based solution
solutions.explanation: Move the useful work into a method so it has a name and can be reused or tested.

solutions.title: Scalable service-style solution
solutions.explanation: For real apps, keep business logic away from input/output so one change does not break the whole program.

tests.name: Structure check
tests.description: The solution should keep core business logic outside Main where possible.

tests.name: Edge-case reasoning
tests.description: The learner should explain at least one invalid input and where it is handled.

rubric.title: Correctness
rubric.description: The project compiles and produces the required output for the smoke test.

rubric.title: Modularity
rubric.description: Business rules live in focused classes or methods, not one giant main method.

rubric.title: Validation
rubric.description: The project prevents at least one invalid state or bad input.

rubric.title: Readability
rubric.description: Names are clear enough to explain in an interview.

rubric.title: Test Thinking
rubric.description: The learner can name normal, edge, and failure test cases.

milestones: Read the scenario and write the expected output.
Compile and run the starter project.
Move one rule into a service/model method if it is not already separated.
Add one validation rule.
Run the smoke test and compare output.
Grade the project using the rubric.
runInstructions: Save each file using the shown path.
Run javac *.java from the folder containing Main.java.
Run java Main.
Compare the console output with the expected output.

capstoneProjects.title: Spring Security Login Flow Simulator
capstoneProjects.goal: Model public and protected routes before wiring a real Spring Boot app.
capstoneProjects.scenario: Spring Security protects routes with authentication and authorization. This plain Java simulator checks the core idea offline.

files.explanation: Main signs in one user and requests a protected page.
User represents authenticated identity and role.
SecurityService decides whether a user can see a protected resource.

flashcards.front: Explain: What is a computer program?
flashcards.back: What is a computer program? belongs to Absolute Computer and Programming Basics. In simple words, it is a tool or idea that helps you understanding computers, programs, Java, and beginner vocabulary. Learn the plain meaning first, then connect it to a tiny Java example, then use it in a small task. Tiny practice: say the idea out loud, then write one small Java example.

Programming means writing clear step-by-step instructions that a computer can follow. The computer does not guess. You must tell it exactly what to do. Tiny practice: say the idea out loud, then write one small Java example.
